blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Limit Evaluation & Indeterminate Forms

body.en: Evaluate one-sided and two-sided limits analytically using direct substitution, factoring, rationalizing, and the squeeze theorem.

label.en: ● The 3-Part Definition of Continuity at a Point & Complete Taxonomy of Graph Cases

body.en:
A function \(f\) is continuous at \(x = c\) if and only if all three conditions of the Continuity Checklist are satisfied:

  1. Condition 1: \(f(c)\) is defined (meaning \(c\) is in the domain of \(f\)).
  2. Condition 2: \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x)\) exists (meaning left and right limits are finite and agree: \(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = L\)).
  3. Condition 3: \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = f(c)\) (the limiting trend matches the actual output).

Failure of any condition produces a specific discontinuity geometry on the Cartesian plane:

  • Case 1 · Continuous: All 3 conditions hold. The curve passes unbroken through \((c, f(c))\).
  • Case 2 · Removable (Hole): Condition 1 fails (undefined at \(c\)), but Condition 2 holds (limit \(L\) exists). The graph has an open ring at \((c, L)\).
  • Case 3 · Removable (Displaced Point): Conditions 1 and 2 hold, but Condition 3 fails (\(f(c) \neq L\)). An open ring sits at \((c, L)\) while a solid dot sits at \((c, f(c))\).
  • Case 4 · Jump Discontinuity: Condition 2 fails because one-sided limits are finite but unequal (\(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)\)). A step break occurs in the graph.
  • Case 5 · Infinite Discontinuity (Vertical Asymptote): Condition 2 fails because one or both one-sided limits grow without bound to \(\pm\infty\).
  • Case 6 · Essential / Oscillating Discontinuity: Condition 2 fails because function values oscillate infinitely rapidly between bounds as \(x\) approaches \(c\).

label.en: ● Precise (ε, δ) Definition of Limit & Rigorous Proofs

body.en:
Definition: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L\) means: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - c| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\).

Rigorous Proof (Linear): Prove that \(\lim_{x\to 3} (4x - 5) = 7\).
Scratchwork: \(|(4x - 5) - 7| = 4|x - 3| < \varepsilon \iff |x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\).
Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Choose \(\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\). If \(0 < |x - 3| < \delta\), then \(|(4x - 5) - 7| = 4|x - 3| < 4\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\right) = \varepsilon\). Thus \(\lim_{x\to 3}(4x - 5) = 7\). \(\blacksquare\)

Rigorous Proof (Quadratic with Bounding): Prove that \(\lim_{x\to 2} x^2 = 4\).
Scratchwork: \(|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2||x + 2|\). Restrict \(\delta \le 1 \implies 1 < x < 3 \implies |x + 2| < 5\). Then \(|x^2 - 4| < 5|x - 2|\). Set \(5|x - 2| < \varepsilon \iff |x - 2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\). Choose \(\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right)\).
Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Set \(\delta = \min\left(1, \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right)\). If \(0 < |x - 2| < \delta\), then \(|x + 2| < 5\) and \(|x - 2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}\). Thus \(|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2||x + 2| < \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right)(5) = \varepsilon\). Hence \(\lim_{x\to 2} x^2 = 4\). \(\blacksquare\)

label.en: ● Precise Definitions of Limits at Infinity & Infinite Limits (with Proofs)

body.en:
1. Limit at Infinity: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to \infty} f(x) = L\) means \(\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists M > 0\) such that \(x > M \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\).

Proof for \(\lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{2x+1}{x+3} = 2\): For \(x > 0\), \(\left|\frac{2x+1}{x+3} - 2\right| = \frac{5}{x+3} < \varepsilon \iff x > \frac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3\). Choose \(M = \max\left(1, \frac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3\right)\). For all \(x > M\): \(\left|\frac{2x+1}{x+3} - 2\right| < \frac{5}{M+3} \le \varepsilon\). \(\blacksquare\)

2. Infinite Limits at a Point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = \infty\) means \(\forall M > 0, \exists \delta > 0\) such that \(0 < |x - c| < \delta \implies f(x) > M\).

Proof for \(\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = \infty\): Let \(M > 0\). Choose \(\delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\). If \(0 < |x| < \delta\), then \(x^2 < \frac{1}{M} \implies \frac{1}{x^2} > M\). \(\blacksquare\)

solution.en: Direct substitution yields \(0/0\). Factor numerator and denominator: \[ \lim_{x\to 3} \frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{(x-3)(x+1)} = \lim_{x\to 3} \frac{x+3}{x+1} = \frac{3+3}{3+1} = \frac{6}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{3}{2}}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — The Three-Part Definition of Continuity & Vertical Asymptotes

body.en: Verify continuity at piecewise boundaries and analyze infinite limits \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = \pm\infty\).

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Find the value of constant \(k\) that makes \(f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^2 + 1 & x \le 2 \\ 3x - 5 & x > 2 \end{cases}\) continuous at \(x = 2\).

solution.en: Require left and right limits to match: \[ \lim_{x\to 2^-} (kx^2 + 1) = 4k + 1, \quad \lim_{x\to 2^+} (3x - 5) = 6 - 5 = 1. \] Set equal: \[ 4k + 1 = 1 \implies 4k = 0 \implies \mathbf{k = 0}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) & Asymptotic Behavior

body.en: State and apply the Intermediate Value Theorem with all conditions (continuity on [a, b]), and evaluate limits at infinity.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

Let \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x - 1\). Explain how the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root in \([1, 2]\).

solution.en:
1. \(f(x)\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous on \([1, 2]\).
2. \(f(1) = 1 - 3 - 1 = -3 < 0\), and \(f(2) = 8 - 6 - 1 = 1 > 0\).
3. Since \(0\) lies strictly between \(f(1) = -3\) and \(f(2) = 1\), by the IVT there must exist at least one \(c \in (1, 2)\) such that \(f(c) = 0\).
